facts.title: Transition to Industrial Sound (1986)
facts.body: After being dropped by his record label and dabbling in goth music (1984-1985), Al Jourgensen restarted his career. In 1986, through Depeche Mode connections, he collaborated with producer Adrian Sherwood. Sherwood's radical remixes (e.g., for Depeche Mode) impressed Jourgensen with their heavy percussion, electronic rhythm, distortion, and tape loops, leading to the industrial-leaning album "Twitch." "But in 1986, through some Depeche Mode connections, he hooked up with producer Adrian Sherwood."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Ministry

facts.title: Unexpected Songwriting Process for "If You Leave" (1986)
facts.body: The band wrote their biggest North American hit, "If You Leave," in a single day at Larabee Studios under extreme time pressure and without their own instruments. Paul Humphreys composed on a piano, which was a rare occurrence, while Andy McCluskey wrote lyrics, a process likened to "Tin Pan Alley Song Riders." "Paul sat down at a piano, which he never does to riveting. And I sat next to him and started writing words and we, like, we've called Tin Pan Ali Song Riders and gathered around the piano."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Golden Age of Synths as told by OMD
facts.name: Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark

facts.title: Beat-Up 1986 Toyota 4x4 Pickup Truck
facts.body: Taylor Hawkins drove a beat-up 1986 Toyota 4x4 pickup truck, which he had bought for $400 in high school. This choice of vehicle, alongside his 2005 Subaru Baja, highlighted his down-to-earth personality and lack of concern for flashy rock star possessions. "He was driving the same beat up 1986 Toyota 4x4 pickup truck that he bought for $400 when he was in high school."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Taylor Hawkins

facts.title: No Doubt (Anaheim, 1986) – Started as Applecore; Original Singer John Spence Committed Suicide Age 18; Tragic Kingdom (1995) 17 Million Copies; Eric Stefani Left for The Simpsons
facts.body: No Doubt was formed in 1986 as a band called Applecore by Eric Stefani and his sister Gwen, later joined by John Spence (who said "no doubt" when he agreed with you — that became the band's name). Spence was the main singer with Gwen on backup. Just before a big showcase for major labels, Spence committed suicide at age 18. After a brief breakup, the band reformed with a new singer named Alan Mead, who didn't last, and then Gwen took over vocals. A self-titled 1992 album flopped (maybe 30,000 copies). A second album called The Beacon Street Collection sold only a few more. Keyboardist Eric Stefani then left to become an animator for The Simpsons, preferring animation to music. Interscope paired the remaining band with producer Matthew Wilder; the resulting Tragic Kingdom came out October 10, 1995 and eventually sold north of 17 million copies worldwide, doing more for ska punk than any other CD. "At last count worldwide sales were somewhere north of 17 million copies."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: A Not-So Brief History of Ska: Part 2
facts.name: No Doubt

facts.title: Big Break on The Tonight Show (1986)
facts.body: In 1986, fellow comedian Jay Leno suggested that booking agents from *The Tonight Show starring Johnny Carson* check out her act at The Improv in Hollywood. facts.title: Dial-a-Song Service (1986 On-Again, Off-Again)
facts.body: Starting in 1986, They Might Be Giants maintained an on-again, off-again service called `Dial-a-Song`. This allowed people to call a specific number, and an answering machine would play a new original song. facts.title: Extreme Volume Causes Structural Damage (1986)
facts.body: In 1986, Motörhead reportedly achieved a volume of 130 decibels during a gig, a level so intense that it "caused structural damage to the variety, theater and cleveland." facts.title: Reclaiming "Louie Louie" Rights (1986)
facts.body: In 1986, Chuck Rubin's legal actions tying up "Louie Louie" prompted a company interested in using the song for a major TV advertising campaign to pressure the song's owner for a resolution. This led to Richard Berry regaining half the publishing rights and full songwriting rights, which he then split with Rubin. "In order to make sure the commercials used Louis Louis, the song's owner gave Berry half the publishing rights and full songwriting rights, which Berry then split with Rubin."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
facts.name: Richard Berry

facts.title: C86 – NME Cassette, May 1986; Young Raw Indie UK Bands; "C" from Cassette Capacity Designations
facts.body: In May 1986, NME included a special cassette with one of their issues featuring young, recently signed bands from various independent British labels. Because blank cassettes had numerical designations (C60 = 60 min, C90 = 90 min), the NME called their 1986 cassette C86. All bands on the tape were young, the music was raw and sometimes primitive, and nothing came from a major label. C86 became shorthand for young, raw, primitive indie rock in the UK. "If you know your cassette culture, you'll know that blank cassettes had special numerical designations."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: C86

facts.body: The artwork for this album prominently features the band standing in front of The Salford Lads' Club on Coronation Street in Manchester. facts.body: Released on November 15, 1986, this album was a monumental success, becoming the first rap album ever to top the charts. It combined punk, rock, rap, funk, and hip hop into a globally successful formula and featured Kerry King of Slayer on guitar, introducing countless millions, especially white suburban kids, to hip hop. "And of course, things completely exploded with their license to Il Album which came out on November 15th in 1986."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Licensed to Ill

facts.body: Released on November 19, 1986, this album was one of the first successful fusions of rap, hip-hop, and rock, appealing to rap, alternative, and mainstream rock fans. Kerry King of Slayer played guitar on the album while concurrently recording *Reign in Blood*. It socially and culturally bridged a huge gap between black and white music fans, who were previously "miles apart." The album became one of the fastest-selling debut albums in history, the first rap record to hit number one on the American album charts, and remains a top-selling back catalog item, selling hundreds of thousands of copies annually. Columbia Records, its distributor for Def Jam, recorded it as their fastest-selling record to that point, eventually selling over ten million copies in the U.S. alone. "Musically, it was one of the first successful fusions of rap, hip hop and rock."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Licensed to Ill

facts.body: Released on November 19th, 1986, this album was a groundbreaking fusion of rap, hip-hop, and rock, appealing to rap, alternative, and mainstream rock fans. It featured Kerry King of Slayer on guitar, who played during the recording of Slayer's "Reign in Blood." The album bridged the gap between black and white music fans and became one of the fastest-selling debut albums in history, being the first rap record to hit number one on the American album charts. It has sold over 10 million copies in the US and remained a top-selling back catalog item for years, moving at least 500,000 copies annually 10-15 years later. The band initially wanted to title it "Don't Be a Faggot." "Licensed to Ill was the first rap record to ever hit number one on the American album charts."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Licensed to Ill

facts.body: The Roland TR-808 drum machine is prominently featured throughout the Beastie Boys' first album, with producer Rick Rubin enhancing its sound and layering it beneath the tracks. "The 808 is all over the first Beastie Boys album."

facts.body: The debut album was initially perceived as a parody of hip hop, leading to the band being pigeonholed as a novelty act for the first eight years of their career. Despite its humorous nature, Rolling Stone magazine acknowledged its significant impact. Profits from this album were later used to fund their G-Sun studio. "License to ill was a parody of hip hop. It was a good one, but it was still a parody."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Licensed to Ill

facts.body: This 1986 album generated substantial income for the Beastie Boys, selling at least 2 million copies annually in the "olden days" before the collapse of record sales due to streaming. The band received "nice checks" from these sales. "The Beastie Boys saw a nice checks from sales of license to ill because this 1986 record sold at least 2 million every year."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Licensed to Ill

facts.body: This album features a gatefold package that unfolds to two square feet (four square feet double-sided) of artwork. The front cover shows the tail of a Boeing 727 with "Beastie Boys" on it and a registration number 3MTA3, which reads "eat me" when held up to a mirror. The back cover depicts the 727 crashed nose-first into a mountain. The design concept of a private jet was developed by Stephen Bierram and World B. Ohms, inspired by stories of Led Zeppelin on their private jet, as described in the biography "Hammer of the Gods." "If you look at the album from the front, we see the tale of a Boeing 727 with Beastie Boys on the tail. The plane has a registration number 3MTA3. But if you hold it up to a mere, it says, eat me."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
